title: Regional integration becomes usable when trade rules are enforceable, defensive instruments disciplined, and people can move
source_unit: World Bank Policy Research Working Paper 11449, Beneath the Surface: Deep Trade Agreements and the Potential of a Deeper AfCFTA
geography: African Continental Free Trade Area and worldwide trade-agreement comparison, with counterfactual estimates for African economies in the sample

observations.period: Worldwide trade agreements; shallow, medium, and deep integration classification

denominator.unit: worldwide trade-agreement corpus classified into three integration-depth clusters

classification.value: trade agreements are classified as shallow, medium, or deep using a clustering algorithm

trade_effects.value: cluster rankings are estimated within a structural-gravity framework to compare trade effects

depth_mechanism.value: the legal and institutional content beneath tariff preferences is associated with whether an agreement produces stronger trade effects

formal_to_usable_gap.value: regional integration on paper does not automatically create usable market access for firms, workers, or consumers

observations.method: Machine-learning clustering of worldwide trade agreements combined with structural-gravity estimation and feature-attribution analysis.
observations.uncertainty: Agreement classifications and estimated trade effects are model-dependent; association between provisions and depth does not by itself establish that a single provision causes observed trade outcomes.
observations.subgroup: Countries, regional agreements, firms, sectors, workers, service providers, and consumers facing different regulatory, customs, mobility, and enforcement barriers.
observations.counterinterpretation: Deep provisions may be adopted by countries that already have stronger institutions, infrastructure, or trade capacity; the observed depth effect may partly reflect selection and implementation quality.

denominator.unit: African Continental Free Trade Area policy counterfactual for African economies in the study sample

baseline_depth.value: AfCFTA is classified as medium in the paper's baseline

deep_counterfactual.value: implementing AfCFTA as a deep agreement is estimated to generate substantial additional trade gains

gdp_result.value: average GDP gain of approximately 0.7 percent for the African economies in the sample
gdp_result.unit: modeled percentage change relative to counterfactual baseline

distributional_boundary.value: the modeled gain is an economy-level counterfactual, not evidence that firms, workers, regions, or households receive equal benefits

observations.method: General-equilibrium counterfactual analysis applied to AfCFTA configurations informed by the agreement-depth classification.
observations.uncertainty: Results depend on model structure, trade elasticities, sectoral responses, implementation assumptions, adjustment costs, and the extent to which formal provisions are actually enforced.
observations.subgroup: African economies, exporting and importing firms, formal and informal businesses, workers in tradable sectors, consumers facing prices and product variety, and regions with different logistics capacity.
observations.counterinterpretation: Aggregate GDP gains can coexist with adjustment losses, concentrated firm power, regional divergence, job displacement, or higher compliance costs for smaller firms; the estimate is not a poverty or welfare result.

observations.period: Agreement provisions associated with deep integration

legal_enforceability.value: stronger legal enforceability is among the provisions most closely associated with deep agreements

trade_defense.value: tighter disciplines on trade-defense instruments are among the provisions most closely associated with deep agreements

visa_provisions.value: visa-related provisions are among the provisions most closely associated with deep agreements

social_translation.value: enforceable rules and mobility can convert regional integration from tariff access into usable opportunities for firms, workers, and service users

observations.method: Feature-attribution methods and counterfactual policy combinations identify provision configurations associated with deep classification.
observations.uncertainty: Feature attribution identifies predictive or correlational contribution within the model, not a clean causal estimate of each legal or visa provision; implementation and political contestation remain open.
observations.subgroup: Cross-border workers, service providers, firms using regional supply chains, smaller enterprises, migrants, border communities, customs agencies, and consumers.
observations.counterinterpretation: Mobility and enforceability provisions can create uneven access, administrative burden, labor-market competition, or political resistance if documentation, social protection, and recognition systems do not travel with people and firms.

related_sources.claim: Official World Bank record for WPS11449, authors, themes, sectors, topics, and reproducibility package.
Bibliographic record and abstract for agreement classification, structural gravity, AfCFTA baseline, 0.7 percent GDP counterfactual, and key provisions.
World Bank reproducibility package and study metadata.

boundary: This record adds regional-integration depth as a legal, mobility, firm, and geopolitical mechanism. It does not establish that AfCFTA implementation will produce the modeled GDP gain, that aggregate trade gains will be equally distributed, or that deep provisions automatically create household welfare, jobs, voice, or consumer affordability.
